strengths: Learning initializations while retaining Sinkhorn refinement addresses a useful practical problem. Combining adversarial synthetic data generation with supervised dual-potential prediction is a plausible contribution beyond dataset-specific learned initializers.

The reported improvements are consistent across four test datasets. Tables 1–2 show approximately 16% and 33% fewer iterations on average at marginal-error tolerances of 1e-3 and 1e-2, respectively. Evaluating marginal feasibility alongside transport-cost errors and wall-clock time strengthens the empirical evidence.

The pipeline is reasonably understandable, with pseudocode, network dimensions, training hyperparameters, and a code link. The appendix provides a sound proof of the objective-value inequality in Proposition 7.
weaknesses: The central contribution of adversarial generation is not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison against a fixed generator or non-adversarial synthetic sampling with the same architecture and labeling budget. Consequently, the benefit attributable to adversarial learning beyond supervised potential prediction remains unclear.

The main convergence experiments compare only against all-ones initialization, omitting the cited initializers of Thornton and Cuturi and an end-to-end comparison with Amos et al. Figure 3 evaluates the alternative training objective using potential MSE, which directly favors the supervised objective and requires careful alignment of additive constants. It does not establish superior Sinkhorn convergence or computational efficiency, particularly after accounting for ground-truth label generation.

The universality claim exceeds the evidence. All experiments use the same 784-point grid, squared Euclidean cost, and epsilon of 0.00025. Transfer across four image families is encouraging, but neither a coverage argument nor challenging distributional stress tests support generalization to arbitrary pairs of fixed-dimensional distributions. The motivation of reusing predictions across regularization strengths is also untested.

Section 3.3 interprets Proposition 7 too strongly: an entropic dual objective-value bound does not establish closeness of the potentials or faster Sinkhorn convergence. At the experimental settings, the bound mnε is approximately 154, whereas the underlying transport costs are bounded by 2. It therefore provides little quantitative justification for the proposed initialization, especially with prediction error and clipping.

The auxiliary claim that the network can independently compute barycenters has only qualitative support. Figure 7 lacks reference barycenters, objective gaps, or runtime comparisons. The error-cancellation argument assumes zero-mean prediction errors without evidence; its expectation identity does not control optimization error when predictions depend on the evolving barycenter.

Despite the useful implementation details, the manuscript omits test-pair counts, independent training-run counts, the construction of uncertainty intervals, and the test-time smoothing constant. Numerical stabilization and timing methodology also need clarification. These omissions limit assessment of robustness and reproducibility.
